name: Naminidil

card.summary: An investigational topical potassium channel opener, developed by Bristol-Myers Squibb as a hair-growth treatment for thinning hair.
card.note: Discontinued at phase II; not marketed.

quick.overview:
Naminidil is a small molecule that Bristol-Myers Squibb developed as a topical treatment for hair loss. Like minoxidil, it is a potassium channel opener, a drug class that has been studied for hair growth.

It was meant to help thinning hair look fuller. A phase II program began in 2001 and was discontinued in 2008, and the compound was never marketed.
quick.how: It is not available as an approved product. Hair-loss communities discuss it as a minoxidil relative, but there is no standard consumer form.
quick.risks: No published clinical results exist, so its safety and effect in people are not documented. It is not approved in any country.

lead: Naminidil (BMS-234303) is an investigational cyanoguanidine that acts as an ATP-sensitive potassium channel opener, developed by Bristol-Myers Squibb for topical treatment of alopecia.[1]

Its goal was the same as minoxidil's, to support hair growth on thinning scalps, though it is chemically a different compound.[1] A patent by inventor Karnail Atwal lists minoxidil, pinacidil and diazoxide as known potassium channel openers with hair-growth activity.[1]
Public records show phase II trials starting in 2001 and the program ending in 2008 without a reported outcome.[1]

chain: Opens potassium channels in follicle tissue
angle.text: Naminidil was designed to improve hair density on thinning scalps in the same pharmacological class as minoxidil. It never reached the market.

paras: Naminidil is a single-enantiomer cyanoguanidine with formula C15H19N5, listed with a 4-cyanophenyl group and a branched alkyl group.[1] It is reported to target SUR1 and SUR2 with Kir6.2 channels.[1]
The name appeared in WHO nomenclature lists in 2002 and 2003. Development records note a topical phase II program in the United States from 2001 until discontinuation in 2008.[1]
No studies found. No trial records or published papers on naminidil are indexed. The only public activity data are patent figures, including measurements in mice.[1]
